shared_context_text:
The spectrum of stiff person syndrome (SPS) spans from the
focal variant of stiff limb syndrome (SLS) to the widespread
involvement observed in progressive encephalomyelitis with
rigidity and myoclonus. Common characteristics comprise ﬂuc-
tuating rigidity of trunk and proximal limb muscles superim-
posed by painful spasms as well as associated autoantibodies,
mainly directed against proteins of inhibitory synapses, such
as glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), glycine receptors, or
amphiphysin.
1–5
Apart from motor impairment, patients are often handicapped
by a characteristic fear of walking or standing unaided, which is
best described as task-speciﬁc phobia and may precede onset of
motor symptoms.
6,7 Furthermore, many patients complain of epi-
sodes resembling gait ignition failure or freezing of gait (FOG). 4,6
The motor manifestations of stiffness, limb posturing, and
FOG-like episodes, together with the relative rareness of the
disorder, make it conceivable that SPS might be misdiagnosed
as atypical parkinsonism, in particular, corticobasal syndrome
(CBS). To illustrate this, we present two cases of established
SLS resembling CBS and discuss the distinguishing features that
may alert the clinician to the correct diagnosis, with its obvious
therapeutic and prognostic implications.

Case 1
This 69-year-old gentleman had a previous medical history of
diabetes type 1 when he presented with gradually progressive,
severe walking difﬁculties. On examination, he displayed
marked stiffness of the right leg with extension posturing and
consecutive gait impairment with difﬁculties turning. Remark-
ably, the leg stiffness immediately disappeared when he assumed
a sitting position (see Video 1). Independent from position,
however, extensor spasms of the legs could be provoked by
plantar touching. Except for hyperhidrosis, the remainder of the
neurological examination was normal, and there was no exag-
gerated startle response, bradykinesia, tremor, or apraxia. Diag-
nostic workup revealed high titers of GAD antibodies and
exaggerated exteroceptive reﬂexes as well as continuous motor
unit activity (CMUA), whereas tumor screening was negative.
He had a good treatment response to diazepam and tizanidine
and remained stable for 12 years, when he noticed a worsening
of his symptom, which responded well on treatment with a
corticosteroid pulse and oral tapering. No new symptoms have
developed during the follow-up of 13 years.

Case 2
A previously healthy gentleman developed persistent pain and
swelling of the left ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joint along with a
progressive gait disturbance at the age of 71. He complained of
stiffness, which started in the left foot, spreading over months to
affect the entire leg and referred to greater difﬁculty walking in
open spaces than down a corridor. Painful leg spasms could be
precipitated by unexpected noise or touch. On examination, he
had reduced facial expression, and repetitive ﬁnger movements
were mildly slow, worse on the left, yet without fatiguing. There
was a marked stiffness of the legs, more pronounced on the left,
and a striatal toe on the left. Hyper-reﬂexia involved both legs,

but there was no weakness. Gait was slow and asymmetric, princi-
pally resulting from stiffness and posturing of the left leg with
excessive knee extension and plantar ﬂexion mainly on attempt-
ing to walk (see Video 2). Overall posture was ﬂexed rather than
lordotic. Investigations revealed high titers of serum GAD anti-
bodies, CMUA, and enhanced exteroceptive reﬂexes. MRI brain
scan was normal apart from possible mild focal bilateral superior
parietal atrophy. FDG-PET found focal cortical hypometabolism
in the sensorimotor region, more prominent on the right. Symp-
toms were unresponsive to levodopa and baclofen, but the painful
spasms responded to intravenous diazepam and immunotherapy
(intravenous immunoglobulin, pulse prednisone, followed by
weaning doses of oral prednisone). On a follow-up of 16 years,
he has become disabled by psoriatic arthritis, whereas stiffness
remains well controlled. He has not developed parkinsonism.
Discussion
Here, we present two cases of an unusual presentation of SPS,
which could have been mistaken for CBS with lower-limb onset. 8
Particularly, some symptoms of SPS may lead to a misdiagnosis of
parkinsonism, especially of atypical forms such as CBS.
Both SPS and parkinsonian conditions feature an increased
muscle tone. Stiffness in SPS is not always bilateral and occa-
sionally involves facial muscles.
1 Stiff limb posturing, as shown
in both examples, can be mistaken for limb dystonia, which is a
characteristic sign of CBS or young-onset Parkinson’s disease.
8,9
Stiffness of facial muscles might resemble parkinsonian hypomi-
mia. Moreover, SPS patients have gait difﬁculties and might
relate episodes resembling FOG (our own observation and
described elsewhere
4,6).
However, the diagnoses of SPS in our patients are supported
by the electrophysiological and serological ﬁndings, treatment
response, and the clinical course on long-term follow-up.
Moreover, some points of a careful clinical examination allow
an early distinction and guide to the correct diagnosis.
Features deﬁning parkinsonism comprise rigidity, postural insta-
bility, rest tremor, and bradykinesia. In contrast to the rigidity and
dystonic posturing observed in CBS, the stiffness in SPS is ﬂuctu-
ating and mostly subsides at rest. The latter is clearly demonstrated
in our cases, where there was no leg stiffness while sitting, but only
when attempting to walk. Moreover, stiffness in SPS is often
superimposed by tonic spasms, which can be easily provoked by
touch or pain or even by forcing the patient to walk unassisted.
Whereas foot deformities or exaggerated startle reﬂex in SPS
might interfere with testing for postural instability by pull test,
SPS patients have neither rest tremor nor bradykinesia. Fatigu-
ing of movement amplitude is a prerequisite of the latter, so
one must not be mislead by pure slowness of movement in the
case of severe stiffness.
10 Additional symptoms frequently
observed in CBS are cortical signs, such as sensory loss, apraxia,
as well touch-sensitive and action myoclonus of the limbs, all of
which are not observed in SPS. Also, SPS patients often have
an exaggerated startle response observed, for example, when
eliciting the head retraction reﬂex. Further clues from history
include a propensity to autoimmunity, especially type 1 diabetes
or thyroid disease.
In conclusion, we wish to point out that SLS might mimic
atypical parkinsonism, especially CBS, at ﬁrst sight. However, if
the clinician is alert to this possibility, there are features that
allow a distinction between these two conditions. Awareness of
this differential diagnosis is important as for treatment implica-
tions and prognosis.
